messages.subject_clean: Errors installing inlabru and fmesher packages
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-INLA group,

I am trying to install inlabru and fmesher packages using the following code, but I receive error messages instead. Unfortunately, I don't know how to resolve.

# Install the fmesher package
library(devtools); install_bitbucket("finnlindgren/fmesher@default")
Installation failed: Couldn't resolve host name

# Install the inlabru
devtools::install_git("https://github.com/fbachl/inlabru.git")
Downloading git repo https://github.com/fbachl/inlabru.git
Installation failed: Error in 'git2r_clone': failed to send request: The server name or address could not be resolved

Your help will be appreciated. My session info can be found below.

Regards,
Andronikos

> I agree that leaving only 1 out when you have around 1 observation per area*time may not be the best.
>
> Probably, the goal of your analysis is not to be able to predict at a single area*time in the future, but more of an overall abundance?
>
> ## Idea / Suggestion
> - L5O: Leave 5 out
> - Compute the true sum of incidences
> - Sample from the posterior and add the samples together for the predicted sum
> - Compare the distribution of the predicted sum to the true value of the sum
>
> Why not take the average of the scores for 3-5 different points? I do not think that would give you a proper scoring rule. I think it is better to look at the probability distribution of the sum of the values, and do a proper scoring rule on that target.
>
> ## Run time of CV (LOO or L5O)
> If you want to run the full Cross-validation, this may take forever. What I would do is to sample points at random to do the prediction scenario on, not sampling the same points twice, and stop when you don't have time to do any more.
>
> ## DIC etc
> I think these measures often give the wrong answer on what model is best, for your kind of models. One thing you can try is to compute the cpo and look at result$cpo$failures; if the sum of the failures is not too large this gives a very good approximation of the LOOCV. Usually, in your kind of models, there are too many failures.
>
> However, sometimes you get a massive difference in DIC or WAIC, like 10000. That gives you a strong hint that one of the models are better.
>
> Kind regards,
> Haakon Bakka

> > > When you don't have enough data to leave out a subset of the analysis as a whole to do validation, cross-validation is one of the few general options you have. Leaving out one year at a time would test the ability of the model to predict that year using the past and future years. In some cases, this may be what you want the model to be good at, and then it's an appropriate check. In other cases it's the spatial (and-or spatio-temporal) prediction ability that matters; then you'd just leave out a region at a time, and not the entire year.
> > > So you may need to ask yourself I what _way_ you want the model to be "good", and then target that aspect in the validation checks.  DIC etc can give general hints, but they're very blunt instruments. Targeted posterior predictive checks tend to give more insight.

In such models, I wouldn't necessarily assign a unit to the model components at all, but there are usually other possible interpretations.
For the Poisson case, the log-link means that each component gives (the log of) a multiplicative change in the response expectations. If you can imagine what the "unit" of the log of a relative change is, then the variance would have the square of that, but I would say that they are both unitless.
For the binomial logic-link case, it's harder to directly interpret, but there is a relation with log-odds-ratios, which again would be unitless.

Finn

Hi,

what is done, it also to introduce the linear predictor itself into the
latent field.

if

y ~ 1 + x

then we have the intercept b0 and the regression coof for x, b1.
additionally we introduce

	eta = b0*1 + b1*x

so the latent field is

to avoid singularity, we add a little noise so that

	eta|... ~ N(b0*1 + b1*x, tiny.noise)

then y[i] only depend on eta[i].

this is also discussed in the original inla-paper, 2009.

If you want the predictions at the data locations, there is no need for a new stack as such predictions will be already computed if asked, just set compute=TRUE in control.predictor().

The 'scale' is the scale for the precision, which is the inverse of the squared standard deviation.

Best,

messages.subject: Help translating BUGS model to INLA model
messages.subject_clean: Help translating BUGS model to INLA model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am modeling bird counts from across North America using a method that is common in the bird population literature.  In my test data set, the counts occurred annually for 48 years, at 223 count circles, which fall within 10 study regions or strata.  The standard model structure for these analyses is described in the PNG image below.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-OiE52R6gqmA/WURpU8uJCBI/AAAAAAAADuE/NrIm8Y48_Qw32wY7g_RHkz0BmrDWX5tMQCLcBGAs/s1600/Untitled.png>

The standard way to evaluate this model is using OpenBUGS.  This is the way people code Eq 1 in OpenBUGS.

#### priors ####

for(i in 1:nstrata){

  B[i] ~ dnorm(muB, tau.B)            # effort effect 1 per stratum

  p[i] ~ dnorm(muP, tau.p)            # effort effect 2 per stratum

  trend[i] ~ dnorm(0, 0.000001)       # temporal trend per stratum

  stratum[i] ~ dnorm(0, 0.000001)     # stratum intercept

  tau.year[i] ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)

  sd.year[i] <- 1 / pow(tau.year[i], 0.5)

  for (t in 1:nyear){

    year[i,t] ~ dnorm(0, tau.year[i]) # random year effect per stratum

  }

}

muB ~ dnorm(0, 0.000001)

muP ~ dunif(-4, 4)

tau.p ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)

tau.B ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)

for (i in 1:nsite){

  site[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.site)        # random circle effect

}

tau.site ~ dgamma(0.001,0.001)

sd.site <- 1/pow(tau.site, 0.5)

tau.overdisp ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)   # observation effect for overdispersion

sd.overdisp <- 1/pow(tau.overdisp, 0.5)

#### likelihood ####

for(i in 1:n.obs){

  count[i] ~         dpois(lambda[i])

  lambda[i] <-       exp(od.log.lambda[i])

  od.log.lambda[i] ~ dnorm(log.lambda[i], tau.overdisp)

  log.lambda[i] <-   stratum[SC[i]] +

                     site[CC[i]] +

                     year[SC[i], Yr[i]] +

                     trend[SC[i]] * (Yr[i] - fixed_yr) +

                     B[SC[i]] * (pow(scaledEffort[i], p[SC[i]])-1) / p[SC[i]]

}

I have been asked to try to evaluate the same model using INLA.  But I am having a hard time specifying the model.  Here are a few of my attempts that I know are incorrect.  This first one runs to completion but, among other things, the effort effect is a modeled with smooths instead of the non-linear functions in the BUGS model. There are probably other problems as well.

form_inla <- count ~ -1 + strataF +       # fixed stratum effect

    f(circle, model="iid", constr=T) +    # random circle-specific intercept

    f(yrBugs, model="iid", group=strataN, constr=T) + # random intercept per

# year per stratum

    yrBugs:strataF +                      # year effect per stratum

    f(inla.group(scaledEffort), model="rw2", group=strataN, constr=F) +

# effort effect per stratum

    f(overdisp, model="iid", constr=T)    # zero-centered random intercept

# for overdispersion

This next one has sigmoidal effort effects, which are closer to what are in the BUGS model, but still sufficiently different.  It runs when there is not a group argument, but crashes when a group argument is added.

form_inla <- count ~ -1 + strataF +       # fixed stratum effect

    f(circle, model="iid", constr=T) +    # random circle-specific intercept

    f(yrBugs, model="iid", group=strataN, constr=T) + # random intercept per

# year per stratum

    yrBugs:strataF +                      # year effect per stratum

    f(scaledEffort, model="sigm", group=strataN, constr=F) +

# effort effect per stratum

    f(overdisp, model="iid", constr=T)    # zero-centered random intercept

# for overdispersion

I would appreciate any help you can offer getting the INLA model specification to match the BUGS specification.  For most model terms, it should be easy enough, yes?  But for the non-linear effort term, I suspect that a new latent model structure might be necessary.  Any ideas?

This analysis is done for roughly 500 species each year.  Analyzing all these models using OpenBUGS takes several months of computing time. INLA could cut this computing time drastically.  Plus an INLA implementation would facilitate a better treatment of spatial patterns in the data (e.g., stationary SPDE, non-stationary SVC model) that are now dealt with in a very crude way using discreet strata (essentially spatial fixed effects).  This work will likely end up in a publication, and I am happy to offer authorship to someone who can help me achieve an INLA implementation.

Thanks!

Tim Meehan

I think p is the only problem that stops this from being fitted with
INLA - if you fixed that to a value, then everything is linear.
Maximising that might not be too difficult, with repeated calls to
INLA, and MCMC is also possible (Håvard waved this pre-print at me a
few weeks ago: https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.07844).

TBH, I would probably try to use a low-order polynomial or a stiff rw2
model, as it'll be close enough, and you're not too worried about the
precise shape of the relationship. Depending on what effort actually
is, log transforming it might be sufficient too (if the observed
abundance should be proportional to effort, then log(effort) will be
an offset on the log scale).

HTH

Bob

This might be a job for our new inlabru package; it iterates linearised versions of non-linear predictors with inla(). It was originally designed to handle variable detection probability models in transact sampling data, but can now handle more general non-linear expressions.  Internally,
It converts the nonlinear parameters/functions to latent Gaussian variables, so can in principle handle more nonlinear parameters than basic MCMC would. The trade off is that the output isn't fully Bayesian, but a hybrid method.

The package website can be found here:
https://sites.google.com/inlabru.org/inlabru/home

We're in the process of releasing a new version with improved syntax, so some of the material may be inconsistent.

Finn

Dear INLA-group,

I am estimating the Bernardinelli et al. (1995,  Stat. Med. 14, 2433-2443) using the code and data provided by Blangiardo and Cameletti. To reproduce my question, please find the code below.

library(maptools); library(sp); library(INLA)

url <- "https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/Ohio_data.zip"
temp <- tempfile()
download.file(url, temp)
unzip(temp, "Ohio_data/OhioRespMort.csv")
data <- read.csv("Ohio_data/OhioRespMort.csv")
unzip(temp, exdir = tempdir())
shapefile <- paste0(tempdir(),"\\Ohio_data\\tl_2010_39_county00")
ohio <- readShapeSpatial(shapefile)
county1 <- data$county
Ohio.adj <- paste0(tempdir(),"\\Ohio_data\\Ohio.graph")

formula.par <- y ~ 1 + f(county,model="bym",graph=Ohio.adj, constr=TRUE) + f(county1,year,model="iid", constr=TRUE) + year
model.par <- inla(formula.par,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
                  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                  control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

m <- model.par$marginals.random[[1]][1:88]
zeta.ST1 <- unlist(lapply(m,function(x)inla.emarginal(exp,x)))
SMR.cutoff<- c(0.0, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1,3)
xi.factor <- cut(zeta.ST1,breaks=SMR.cutoff,include.lowest=TRUE)
m <- model.par$summary.random[[2]][1:88,2]
int.cut <- c(-0.008,-0.001,0,0.001,0.006)
int.factor <- cut(m,breaks=int.cut,include.lowest=TRUE)
# spatial effect
data.ohio <- attr(ohio, "data")
attr(ohio, "data")=data.frame(data.ohio, xi=xi.factor)
spplot(obj=ohio, zcol= "xi", col.regions=gray(3.5:0.5/4),main="")
# differential effect
data.ohio <- attr(ohio, "data")
attr(ohio, "data") <- data.frame(data.ohio, int=int.factor)
spplot(obj=ohio, zcol= "int",col.regions=gray(3.5:0.5/4),main="")

Mapping the differential effect shows the deviation from the grand temporal trend. So far so good but, first, how do I know which deviation is "significantly" different from the grand temporal trend?

Second, when I would like to extend the model with additional independent varibles can they be either temporally varying (e.g. annual income data combined into a single vector) or temporally constant (e.g. the same variable will be repeated for each year and combined into a single vector) for the observation time?

Many thanks,Macro

messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

You: "Mapping the differential effect shows the deviation from the grand temporal trend. So far so good but, first, how do I know which deviation is "significantly" different from the grand temporal trend? "

## What parts of an iid effect is significant
This is not easy to answer. It is not easy to know what is the correct equation for representing the idea "significant".

The simplest answer would be to look at those where the 95% CI do not contain zero. These are in some sense significant, but you have the problem of "multiple hypothesis testing". As long as you are very careful with your interpretation, this approach may be helpful.

CAUTION!!! If you want to think about significantly different from zero, you must be careful with your prior. The default prior is not appropriate, as that prior is already "significantly not zero", and pushes the result towards significant results. You should use a conservative PC-prior instead.
>> inla.doc("pc.prec")

## "Significance" through model comparison
If you have a good criterion, you can remove parts of your model and talk about "significant" in the sense of "the data is modeled significantly better" with this part than without it.

## extend the model with additional independent varibles
Both of your examples sound like covariates to me. You can add as many linear covariates as you want, no matter how these numbers look in space or time. It is very common to have spatially or temporally structured covariates. You may get confounding between the covariates and the random effects though.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Code example to define adjacency as points within a certain cutoff:

n <- 30
xy <- cbind(runif(n), runif(n))
cutoff <- 0.1
j <- lapply(1:n, function(i)
   setdiff(which(sqrt((xy[,1]-xy[i,1])^2 +
                      (xy[,2]-xy[i,2])^2)<cutoff),i))
nn <- sapply(j,length)
graph <- sparseMatrix(i=rep(1:n, nn), j=unlist(j),
                       x=rep(1, sum(nn)), dims=c(n,n))
image(graph)

The 'graph' object can be supplied in Besag's like models as
   f(..., graph=graph)

best,
Elias
